item.title: Can VIBE Drive Development? Threats and Opportunities
item.dc:creator: Mayukh Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Vibe coding needs a foundation that veterans of the craft can respect. One way forward is to treat VIBE as an acronym that treats it as a philosophy of responsibility: Verifiable, Interpretable, Balanced, Evolvable.
item.content:encoded:
In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy, the computer scientist who had once steered Tesla’s AI division, introduced a phrase that quickly seeped into both Silicon Valley Slack threads and college dorm rooms: vibe coding. At first it sounded like a joke, another meme-friendly coinage that belonged next to “YOLO”a investing and “fail fast.” But within weeks, Merriam-Webster had listed it as slang, and The New York Times was running stories of non-coders building apps by simply chatting with large language models. Suddenly, “going with the vibes” was not about playlists or weekend moods, but about software development itself.

To understand vibe coding, you have to picture a developer setting aside the rigid syntax of Java or Python and instead conversing with a chatbot. The machine produces code, the human accepts it, tests it, and asks for refinements. The emphasis shifts from construction to direction, from keystrokes to conversation. Karpathy himself described the process as “forgetting that the code even exists” and instead leaning into a rhythm of prompts and prototypes. The danger and thrill of vibe coding lies in this surrender. Unlike pair programming or even Copilot-assisted typing, vibe coding asks the human to stop micromanaging and to let the AI fill in the scaffolding.

Vibe coding has already drawn thoughtful attention with Communications readers,1,3,8 with editorial content describing the effect of early experiments on the work of programmers and product managers. But for this exploratory use of vibe coding to become a permanent part of the craft, it needs enough discipline to avoid drifting into slopware. This Opinion column therefore examines both the opportunities that vibe coding opens for wider participation and rapid prototyping, and the threats it poses in the form of fragility, opacity, and undisciplined software practice.

Once we recognize this shift, the path leads toward vibe-driven development (VDD), a framework that seeks to bring order to the chaos, discipline to the improvisation. The story of computer science is full of such inflection points, where wild freedom was later tamed by structure. In the 1960s, spaghetti code dominated early software projects until Edsger Dijkstra’s famous letter, “GoTo Statement Considered Harmful,” inspired programmers to rethink their practices. In the 1990s, object-oriented design became the lodestar. In the 2000s, Agile and SOLIDb principles emerged as antidotes to bloat and rigidity. Each time, structure saved creativity from collapsing under its own weight. The same must happen with vibe coding.

The Expanded Form of VIBE

If vibe coding is to evolve into something credible, it cannot remain a slang term tossed around in incubators. It needs a foundation, something that veterans of the craft can respect. One way forward is to treat VIBE as an acronym:

VIBE = Verifiable, Interpretable, Balanced, Evolvable:

  • Verifiable: Any AI-generated code must be testable, measurable, and accountable. The early days of vibe coding often ignored this, leading to software that worked in demos but broke in production. Verification anchors vibes to reality. It also calls for a small degree of care around copyright, since the legal status of model-generated code is still unsettled. Simple provenance checks and quick license scans help keep this in view.

  • Interpretable: Black-box code is a breeding ground for bugs and vulnerabilities. VIBE insists that even if the AI writes the code, the human must be able to interpret its logic. This draws from the SOLID principle of Single Responsibility, clarity instead of cleverness.

  • Balanced: Vibe-driven work should balance speed with maintainability, novelty with stability. This is the antidote to the excesses of “just ship it” culture. Balance recalls the clean code philosophy that prioritizes readability instead of wizardry.

  • Evolvable: Refactoring must not be an afterthought but part of the workflow. Codebases written under the influence of vibes must be designed to evolve, not ossify. Here we borrow directly from the SOLID principle of Open/Closed: software should be open to extension but closed to reckless modification. Some models tend to recreate framework code rather than use the intended abstractions, which erodes reusability. Regular refactoring and a preference for clean, modular APIs help the system grow without losing shape.

In short, vibe coding may be born from spontaneity, but VIBE-driven development asks it to mature into a philosophy of responsibility.

The Historical Echo

The excitement around vibe coding is not new in spirit. History is littered with movements that promised to democratize programming. In the 1960s, COBOL was pitched as a language “any manager could read.” In the 1980s, Apple’s HyperCard allowed non-programmers to build interactive applications with drag-and-drop stacks. In the 2010s, the “no-code” movement reemerged with platforms like Bubble and Webflow.

Each of these moments carried the same utopian hope: that one day, to tell a computer what to do, you would only need to speak in plain language. Karpathy’s quip that “the hottest new programming language is English” echoes a dream that stretches back to Alan Turing’s own musings on natural language as a programming interface.

But each wave also hit the same wall: complexity. COBOL programs grew unwieldy. HyperCard stagnated because serious developers dismissed it. No-code platforms empowered hobbyists but rarely powered billion-dollar infrastructures. The threat today is that vibe coding, if left unchecked, may meet the same fate: lots of novelty, little durability.

Opportunities in the Vibe Era

And yet, the opportunities are undeniable. Kevin Roose, a New York Times journalist with no professional coding background, built small applications using vibe coding: an app that analyzed his fridge and suggested packed lunches, a tool that generated shopping lists. Amateurish? Perhaps. But they embodied a profound shift: the barrier to entry had collapsed. What once required years of study could now be prototyped over a weekend.

Startups have already taken note. Y Combinator reported that a quarter of its Winter 2025 batch ran codebases that were 95% AI-generated.6 For cash-strapped founders, vibe coding is not just fun, it is survival. Why hire a team of ten when two people and a chatbot can build a minimum viable product? The vibes are, quite literally, venture capital’s new fuel.

This democratization mirrors another historical moment: the rise of open source in the 1990s. Back then, Linux allowed anyone, anywhere, to contribute to the world’s most ambitious operating system. Today, vibe coding allows anyone, anywhere, to create functional software without credentials. The creative floodgates are wide open.

The Threats Beneath the Surface

But open floodgates also drown fields. Critics warn that vibe coding produces fragile, insecure, and inscrutable code. Simon Willison, a seasoned open source programmer, bluntly stated: “Vibe coding your way to a production codebase is clearly risky.”2 The problem is not just that AI may hallucinate functions or fabricate fake reviews (as Roose discovered), but that the resulting code is often unmaintainable.

The dangers resemble the early days of assembly-line software in the 1970s, when productivity soared but quality plummeted. Back then, “software crisis” became the watchword, as bugs, overruns, and crashes plagued the industry. If vibe coding follows the same trajectory, proliferation without discipline, it risks triggering a modern version of that crisis, this time at AI speed.

Security adds another layer of concern. A 2024 large-scale study indicated AI-generated code often contained vulnerabilities that were subtle, non-obvious, and difficult for non-experts to detect.9 In an era where software runs hospitals, banks, and cars, trusting vibes over verification borders on negligence.

Refactoring as a Ritual

One way to avert disaster is to elevate refactoring into the very DNA of VDD. In traditional practice, refactoring is the quiet craft of cleaning up messy code without changing its behavior. British software developer Martin Fowler once likened it to gardening, where you prune branches, rearrange stems, and guide the growth so it stays healthy.4

In vibe coding, this becomes even more urgent. Since the AI writes with little concern for style, humans must step in not just to refactor once, but continuously. Think of it as pair programming where one partner is a machine that never learned etiquette. Every commit must be an opportunity to enforce clarity, modularity, and SOLID discipline.

If vibe coding is jazz, refactoring is the sheet music that ensures future musicians can still play the tune. Without it, today’s improvisation becomes tomorrow’s chaos.

VDD: A Framework for Explainable Vibes

So, what does VDD look like in practice? It begins with four stages, aligned with VIBE:

  • Testing and Verification (Verifiable): Unit tests, integration tests, and automated checks must accompany every generation cycle. Code without tests is vibes without proof.

  • Interpretation and Documentation (Interpretable): Before accepting code, developers must ensure they can explain its logic, at least at a high level. This transforms black boxes into glass boxes.

  • Prompting with Purpose (Bounded): Developers must frame requests with care, keeping the prompt bounded by giving enough detail to guide the model while preserving flexibility. A sloppy prompt produces sloppy code.

  • Refactoring and Extension (Evolvable): Each iteration should include explicit refactoring, not as a luxury but as a contractual obligation. Only then can the system evolve without rot.

This mirrors the clean code ethos: functions that do one thing, classes that bear clear names, systems that are legible. The irony of vibe coding is that it tempts us to throw these principles away. Vibe-driven development insists we bring them back, even more rigorously.

The Human Factor

One overlooked dimension of vibe coding is psychological. Many developers describe the experience as liberating, less typing, more ideation. It recalls Alan Kay’s 1977 dream of computers as “metamedia,” amplifiers for human thought.5 Yet liberation can slip into complacency. When an AI writes every line, developers may lose the intimate knowledge of systems that once made debugging second nature.

This is not unlike the pilots of the 1980s who, flying increasingly automated planes, grew dependent on autopilot systems. The result was “automation complacency,” a contributing factor in several accidents.7 Software engineering faces a similar risk: if vibe coding reduces coders to prompt jockeys, will they still know what to do when the vibes go wrong?

Closing the Loop

Every revolution in computing forces us to renegotiate the boundary between human and machine. In the 1940s, programmers wired plugboards. In the 1960s, they punched cards. In the 1980s, they typed into glowing CRTs. In 2025, they talk to chatbots. The interface keeps shifting, but the underlying tension remains the same: creativity versus control, freedom versus responsibility.

Vibe-driven development offers one possible synthesis. It allows us to embrace the spontaneity of vibes while embedding the rigor of verification, interpretation, balance, and evolvability. It does not reject AI creativity but channels it, much as SOLID principles once channeled the chaos of object oriented sprawl.

The opportunity is vast: more people building more ideas faster than ever before. The threat is equally clear: brittle codebases, opaque systems, and an abdication of accountability. Whether vibe coding becomes a historical footnote like HyperCard or a foundational shift like open source depends on how seriously we take the discipline of VDD.

The vibes are strong. The question is whether we can make them sustainable.

item.title: Une Vie En Rose
item.dc:creator: J.I. Rime
item.description: Efforts for conservation started bubbling up as memory of the digital overload faded.
item.content:encoded:
The position was evasively titled “archival specialist,” and the job requirements listed off dead technologies and languages alike. On their first day, Milo stood in front of a rusty, dented, black storage cabinet.

“That’s the beast,” said the manager as he made his way out of the office. Once he left, there was nothing else but Milo, their desk, silence, and the cabinet.

It towered over them. Inside, a column of decrepit computers stacked on uneven racks. It must have been centuries since these had been turned on. Despite having spent years assiduously studying ancient technologies, Milo barely recognized the hardware, which made the challenge of data retrieval even more interesting to them.

The newly appointed archival specialist spent their first week examining the material. It was tempting to simply press the power button and hope for the best, but half-melted plastic shells and scratched-out aluminium parts did not indicate safety. There was precious data inside each of the disks still lodged within these rough-edged machines—being brisk carried a risk Milo could not take, even though they could barely contain their enthusiasm handling these rare relics, fingers buzzing at every key press.

The “nothing left behind” policy had been in place for so long that no one remembered exactly when it began. It had led to the erasure of millennia of human existence and culture to remedy the unmanageable amount of stuff consistently created by a species that could not stop itself from making.

But now, as the memory of this digital overload faded, efforts for conservation started bubbling up. Activists fought to frame preservation as resistance, and in some places, they succeeded. When machine artifacts were pieced together, dug up, or simply found, they were no longer immediately destroyed. Milo trained to sort through the useful and the useless, to spot value in the discarded, to understand the essential and the superfluous.

So, Milo cleaned these computers with careful fingers, clearing dust and debris, re-attaching disconnected pins and boards, until finally, one machine was ready to be turned on.

For a few agonizing seconds, nothing happened.

An unhappy mechanical rumble growled, followed by a low purring hum. A small LED pin turned green before flickering back to darkness.

Once this first stride was made, it was not long before the archival specialist could access what was left of the hard drives. Most files were encrypted or incomplete. Some held phantoms of databases of which the meaning had long been forgotten, and some used languages no one had spoken in eons. Diligently, Milo made their way through the digital rubble.

The largest file was tucked under a long path name. It was a video file, ready to be consumed by modern eyes in all its inefficient storage requirements.

The image was black and white. Cracks faded in and out from the corners. There was a man behind a microphone. He looked solemn, like he was preparing to give the performance of a lifetime. He raised his hand, commanding the orchestra to begin. The audio was clearly altered, having been converted, compressed, or damaged in some other way. The sound was distorted and echoed as if it was recorded in a large hall.

The man behind the microphone began to sing. The melody was regal, but delicate, almost like a prayer. The singer hit each consonant with brio, like his mouth was a percussion instrument. Milo was fascinated; it was like he didn’t even need to breathe, but still pronounced each syllable perfectly. He must have been an acclaimed performer. The music died down after one song, cutting to black abruptly. The room was silent again, aside from the buzz of the computer.

* * *

“I’m not sure it’s right,” I say with a wince.

The three of us sit around my desk, elbow to elbow on our swivel chairs. Jean brushes my concerns off with a hand gesture. “No one will see it or even know it exists.”

“Although…” Guy interrupts, “maybe they should? Can we add a link in the Readme on the repository?”

His eyes are shining with an excitement I find altogether disturbing. I shut him down: “That’s definitely against our agreement with the National Archive Institute, and honestly, borderline unethical.”

We had been granted access to the training data we needed via a partnership with the NAI. This agreement benefited both parties: We got to train a cutting-edge model, and they got to use its outputs in an exhibition with our common goal being to recreate historical speeches of which recordings had been lost or damaged.

“What’s the harm?” asks Jean. “I’m the only one here who could be offended, and I want to hear that. The model is already trained, and we have all the inputs we need. It’s one line of code for five minutes of trailblazing weirdness.”

I’m still not convinced. Guy pokes my arm. “You don’t even have to see it if it makes you uncomfortable. And we can delete it immediately!”

I don’t have any arguments to counter that. If we are the only ones to see whatever the output will be, it’s almost like it hasn’t happened, right?

So, I run the command. It will take less than an hour to generate the full file with the matching video. Our model uses timbral transfer to match a person’s voice onto another. Traditionally, we would use actors to read archive speeches before applying the real speakers’ vocal identity to them, but here, we transfer the speaker’s voice onto a melody. We got the bare vocal line by running a simple source-separation algorithm on a recording off of YouTube. And just like that, the console log on my terminal window grows over our lunch break, as our secret experiment is carried out quietly.

When the processing stops, a single video file appears in an output folder. Jean and Guy wheel their chairs next to me again, eyes locked on my 15-inch laptop screen.

”We’re only watching it once,” I declare under the misguided assumption they would listen to me, “and then in the bin it goes!”

I hear Guy whisper something like “buzzkill,” but he is quickly distracted by the footage starting to play on my computer. We sit there, wide-eyed. The speaker raises a hand, and I cringe. Then, he starts singing, and Jean chuckles. Did I run a model just to make a man laugh?

The video feels absurd, like a portal into an alternate reality, or the curtains being raised on a play of poor taste. Like an anachronistic painting hanging in Versailles, or the drunken dream of someone who has just watched The Sound of Music. It is everything I did not want it to be, and yet, a part of me revels at how convincing the output of our model is.

On my computer screen, a despot sings:

Quand il me prend dans ses bras, et me parle tout bas, je vois la vie en rose.

A nonsensical piece of fabricated history: no meaning, no harm. Unseen by the world outside of this room.

item.title: Securing Global Law Enforcement Networks Against Cyberattacks
item.dc:creator: David Geer
item.description: Police departments can run afoul of mandates under the U.S. Criminal Justice Information Services Security Policy and the EU Law Enforcement Directive while operating legacy codebases.
item.content:encoded:
Cyber attackers routinely target police departments across the globe. Threat actors can encrypt 911 computer-aided dispatch (CAD) tools and breach police station databases to steal confidential files. System outages can take down emergency call lines, freeze access to forensic evidence, and stall cross-border record checks.

One such breach occurred on March 20, 2026, when a file sharing platform that Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto’s office used to transfer litigation case files to opposing counsel was hit, according to the Los Angeles Times and other outlets. The unauthorized access leaked 7.7 terabytes of sensitive police records across 337,000 files, including officer personnel records, witness medical histories, internal affairs files, and unredacted criminal complaints, some of which subsequently surfaced online, but did not compromise core police infrastructure.

An official statement from the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) noted that the intrusion remained isolated to the City Attorney’s external server and affected files from closed civil lawsuits.

“LAPD is aware of an incident within the LA City Attorney’s Office, where unauthorized individuals gained access to a digital storage system,” the statement said. “This digital storage contained discovery documents from previously adjudicated or settled LAPD civil litigation cases. The breach does not involve any LAPD systems or networks. We take this incident very seriously and are working with the LA City Attorney’s Office to gain access to the impacted files to understand the full scope of the data breach. LAPD is committed to safeguarding its sensitive personnel and investigative information.”

The attack was attributed to WorldLeaks, a cyber-extortion group, which publicly claimed responsibility for the intrusion. Investigators have yet to verify the precise entry point into the City Attorney’s storage system, but security analysts said that WorldLeaks usually breaks in via valid credentials or exposed Web services missing multi-factor authentication. Rather than deploying ransomware, the group generally conducts reconnaissance, moves laterally, steals vast caches of restricted files, and threatens public exposure on its leak site.

The breach underscores how external software can compromise confidential police records whenever access controls and monitoring fall short.

Targeting Police Infrastructure and Vendor Platforms

Anar Israfilov, founder of cybersecurity firm Cyberoon Enterprise Corporation, said criminals target law enforcement networks because connected systems house criminal intelligence, legal records, evidence, and 911 response tools. Attackers include ransomware syndicates looking for leverage, hacktivists, organized crime groups searching for witness rosters, and state-sponsored actors seeking intelligence, said Israfilov.

High-profile incidents highlight several distinct actors or actions:

Ransomware Syndicates. Law enforcement agencies took down the LockBit ransomware syndicate in February 2024, dismantling a prolific network that regularly hit municipal police departments, courts, and public-safety software vendors worldwide.

Hacktivists and Crime Groups. A September 2022 intrusion by the hacktivist collective Guacamaya compromised military and police institutions across Latin America, leaking internal emails and records.

State-Sponsored Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). From May 2021 through February 2022, the state-backed threat group APT41 breached at least six U.S. state government networks housing police and public-safety infrastructure, exploiting vulnerable Web applications for long-term espionage.

Because law enforcement operations run on interconnected digital networks, penetrating a single entry point can hand threat actors access to cross-border intelligence feeds, informant registries, and active evidence files. This structural division of public safety IT creates significant operational security gaps.

According to Israfilov, technical prevention responsibilities are often divided between departments. Law enforcement officers may be responsible for the systems they use, while the local city department may be responsible for infrastructure issues. Vendors will be responsible for third-party platforms used in the processes and the courts are accountable for legal discoveries, said Israfilov.

When security duties split among separate organizations, enforcement breaks down, turning external vendor platforms into unchecked entry points into sensitive data pipelines, he said.

Attack Vectors and System Vulnerabilities

“The most common entry point is weak identity control, especially orphaned or poorly managed accounts with elevated permissions to the critical systems. Third-party tools like legal discovery and evidence systems can also create risk if they do not use strong [phishing-resistant] authentication or proper identity federation,” said Kishore Bitra, lead, collaboration engineering team at Baltimore City Information & Technology.

Advisories from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the SANS Institute repeatedly highlight identity management failures as a primary route into local public-safety networks.

“When attackers get in, older on-premises systems usually fail first. Flat networks make it easier for attackers to move around, which can quickly affect file shares, Active Directory, and user workstations,” said Bitra.

Lacking internal microsegmentation, a breached workstation or unpatched web tool would let intruders pivot across an entire municipal network.

Wanderson Castilho, chief executive officer of Enetsec, a digital forensics and cybercrime investigation firm, said the primary security gaps lie in legacy hardware, outdated software, weak passwords, excessive access privileges, and poorly secured agency-vendor connections.

These technical flaws multiply when public safety agencies attempt to connect modern cloud-hosted discovery platforms directly to legacy database architectures.

Incident Response Sequences

“The first goal is to protect emergency dispatch and keep services running. Instead of shutting everything down, teams should isolate the problem by revoking active sessions, blocking risky sign-ins, and disabling compromised vendor connections,” said Bitra.

Focusing on containment rather than total shutdowns keeps 911 CAD tools online while forensic isolation occurs, a process relying on pre-configured failover protocols designed to isolate compromised software without severing emergency field communications.

“Then, affected service accounts should be turned off and compromised endpoints rebuilt using clean images. Meanwhile, dispatch should continue through backup systems such as isolated communication tools or mobile-managed devices on separate networks so emergency traffic is not interrupted,” said Bitra.

Such a phased recovery workflow keeps threat actors from maintaining a foothold inside core police infrastructure during remediation.

Budgetary and Compliance Barriers

“Public agencies often cannot afford to replace legacy systems all at once due to various reason[s] including the operational budget. Because of that, they keep old platforms running and add vendor integrations, middleware, and scripts on top of them,” said Bitra.

Budget constraints force municipal IT teams to layer custom middleware and scripts around aging databases instead of installing unified modern architectures, making consistent security policy enforcement difficult, he said.

“That creates a compliance problem because older systems usually do not support modern encryption, logging, or authentication standards well. Agencies end up trying to wrap security around fragile legacy systems, which increases complexity, technical debt, and audit risk,” said Bitra.

As a result, departments run afoul of mandates under the U.S. Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Security Policy and the EU Law Enforcement Directive (LED) while operating legacy codebases. CJIS mandates controls for protecting police data, including multi-factor logins, data encryption, and access logs. Meanwhile, the LED sets data-protection and tracking rules across European law enforcement agencies.

Isolating Vendor Tools Within Resource Limits

“Every vendor tool housing police records, discovery documentation, pieces of evidence, or HR data must be regarded as an element of law enforcement attack surface. If the third-party [provider] accesses police information, such access must be segmented, kept under supervision, restricted in time, and subject to auditing,” said Israfilov.

In the end, protecting public-safety networks demands treating every vendor connection as a potential breach point, experts said. Enforcing zero-trust network access, identity federation, tight segmentation, and routine vendor audits allows agencies to safeguard evidence and emergency operations without exceeding municipal budgets.

David Geer is a journalist who focuses on issues related to cybersecurity. He writes from Cleveland, OH, USA.

item.title: Core Concepts in Infrastructure Cost Management
item.dc:creator: Doug Meil
item.description: There is a benefit to the clarity that comes with knowing what was racked and the associated costs.
item.content:encoded:
“All that glitters is not gold.” – William Shakespeare

“. . . but all that glitters and blinks must have a cost center” – Doug Meil

When discussing and comparing on-premise and cloud deployment patterns a decade ago, there would have been a straight line drawn from the first to the second: On-premise was the past and cloud computing was the future, even if people weren’t entirely sure what “cloud computing” was at the time. It is worth re-examining the strengths and weaknesses of both deployment modalities, especially given some notable movements back to on-premise deployments.

On-Premise Cost Management

At the risk of stating the obvious, “on-premise” in the context of this post refers to deployments either within an organization’s physical premises (office or datacenter) or a third party co-located commercial datacenter. Equipment might be purchased or leased, but being on-premise generally refers not just to bare metal servers, but to racks, cables, power supplies, top of rack networking, routers, cooling, raised floors, physical security, and everything else that goes with running a functioning and stable computing environment.   

On-premise deployments are sometimes viewed as inflexible and static; however, they can be quite adaptable when commodity hardware is paired with infrastructure as service frameworks and container frameworks for automated deployments of configurations and software releases. Being comparatively static is true enough as new equipment needs time to be provisioned, but the “static-ness” of the environment is point-in-time, not a permanent condition. The top environment management and scaling challenges are typically:

  1. Choice / Lifespan of Hardware
    1. Especially with purchased equipment, decisions regarding hardware (CPU/GPU, storage, networking) have years of impact, both in terms of technical solution delivery and financials (capital expenses, depreciation). 
  2. Dev and QA Environments
    1. Sizing a production environment is one matter, but properly sizing lower environments can be a challenge—specifically justifying the budgets and proposed/expected utilization to management.
  3. Shared Environment Management
    1. Data and analytic environments are designed to bring data together across sources and teams, but ensuring everybody gets their fair share of resources (and is appropriately paying for it) isn’t always easy. 
  4. Site Failover and Disaster Recovery
    1. This is a particularly hard problem because a fully built-out environment just sitting around waiting to get used is something that most organizations cannot afford. 
    1. This all too often turns into a paper exercise for most organizations.

There is a benefit to the clarity that comes with knowing what was racked and the associated costs. What you see in the racks is exactly what you have.

Cloud Cost Management

Given the complexities of managing on-premise environments, it can be tempting to assume that moving to the cloud will be an easier path because someone else can manage the infrastructure. As with so many things in life the answer is “it depends,” and it especially depends on which pain points are prioritized and which specific cloud features are being leveraged. There is truth in the saying “the cloud is just somebody else’s computer,” but this does not adequately capture the complexity of public cloud platforms like Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud, which are not merely a sets of servers in somebody else’s datacenter, but a vast array of services, many of which are provided by the cloud platform vendor, and some are provided by third parties.   

How does one manage a cloud environment? As with on-premise deployments, looking at costs is a good place to start and the major cloud platforms have built-in cost management dashboards. Below is a screenshot of Azure Cost Analyzer from documentation: 

There are a lot of great numbers and graphs in this dashboard, so it might seem at first glance that our cost management problems are solved. Let’s take a look and find out. 

Service Utilization

Looking closer at the example screenshot provides a useful summary of services, providing a stack-rank of cost categories: Virtual Machines in first place, and Storage in second place. This is useful insight, but this also raises further questions: 

  1. Virtual Machines. Money is clearly being spent on compute, but on how many VMs? What are they doing? Are they fully utilized? 
  2. Storage. “Storage” in cloud computing can mean everything from local storage to VMs to cloud storage services, and charges can be accrued for writing, storing, and reading data. What exactly is being stored where, and at what cost? Storage services also have optional replication and redundancy capabilities available for up-charges.

None of these initial questions address how well this cloud-hosted solution is functioning. Performance diagnostics and tuning are enormous topics outside the scope of this post, but should still be mentioned because they wind up invariably having a cost impact somewhere. So many questions from a single pie chart! Getting access to diagnostic logs, as well as detailed billing records, are highly recommended for deeper analysis.

It should also be clear by this point that pretty much all the core on-premise challenges still remain in the cloud, but there are just a more tools that can be brought to bear. One construct is to configure appropriate “resource groups” around services and provisioned resources, which can align on major groups of functionality for solutions. Such reporting can be seen in the lower right-hand corner of the high-level cost dashboard, though in the example data nearly all the costs are rolling up to a single resource group.  Resource and activity tagging can also be used for more detailed breakdowns (e.g., function = ABC, department = XYZ).

First-generation cloud deployments generally looked like the above and consisted primarily of VMs and and storage. Today, however, higher-level services are often driving the largest expenditures—especially data and analytic services (for example, Databricks and Snowflake)—and this presents another level of management and observability requirements. A fundamental challenge when building with cloud services is that it is often difficult to know exactly how much something will cost. While cloud services offer flexibility, they also introduce a level of complexity that is under-appreciated.   

Understanding the difference between actual costs vs. amortized costs also matters. Cloud resources and services can often be purchased (or reserved) in blocks with discounts. This can be useful where workloads requirements are better understood, but it also increases complexity of reporting with respect to “cash out the door” vs. reserved resource/service utilization. 

Service-Detail Utilization

To understand what is happening within any given cloud service will require access to service-specific activity and billing records, as well as a thorough understanding of the constructs of the service. Using Databricks as an example, there are major service components such as:

  1. Unity Catalog — the overarching catalog for assets (data and code).
  2. Compute — classic compute for notebooks, which execute in the customer account and accrue cloud VM and Storage charges plus Databricks runtime charges, and “serverless,” which executes entirely in the Databricks control plane but at a higher rate of Databricks runtime charges. 
  3. SQL Warehousing — classic (customer account), serverless.
  4. AI functions — SQL functions, Genie spaces for LLMs, coding assistants, etc.

As all of this may execute entirely within a single cloud resource group, proper tagging becomes critical to differentiate activity and billing from a variety of teams, workloads, and stages (for example, Dev/QA/Prod). Otherwise, developers and administrators will be flying blind. The cost summary of the service will be visible, of course, but that isn’t enough to manage a solution, much less an enterprise rollout.

Adding to the pressure is that it often is not easy to see what cloud-based solutions cost until they have been built. Service-level utilization analysis and tagging is truly a skill within a skill. 

Haven’t We Been Here Before?

Today people can joke about a server running under someone’s desk, but up until roughly the 1980s that would have been highly aspirational, if not science fiction. In the very old days, computing time often was leased on shared systems because only the largest organizations could afford not just to own their own computers but also to build out and operate datacenters to house them. Owning and operating one’s own computing environment represented not only a significant strategic advantage for purpose-built systems, but also operational control and stability. There were good reasons on-premise systems deployments were preferred by so many, once they became economically feasible. 

Public cloud computing appeared in the late 2000s and took hold the following decade. When dynamic resource provisioning and scaling is combined with the wide breadth of services available, this modality can be an especially powerful paradigm. This, however, comes with the age-old tradeoff of vendor lock-in; if a cloud platform decides to raise the rates on a critical dependency, in the short-term there often isn’t much of a choice other than to absorb those costs.      

It should not come as a surprise, then, that there have been some notable examples in the “back-to-on-premise” movement. If workloads are thoroughly understood and predictable, on-premise deployments still can represent not only a cost-effective approach, but one with control down to bare metal if one so chooses. 

All of this, whether on-premise or in the public cloud, is part of effective FinOps (financial operational analytics). Whichever deployment path is taken, the responsibility of environment management never ends, and there are no free lunches.

References

2. State of Tokenomics: September 2026. FinOps Foundation.

3. Engro Technologies. Cloud Repatriation: Why Some Enterprises Are Moving Back On-Prem? LinkedIn.

4. Wikipedia. All That Glitters is Not Gold.

item.title: Another Proposal to Rename AI
item.dc:creator: Mario Antoine Aoun
item.description: A proposal to use Super Computer Intelligence as an alternative name for artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
In this post, I introduce Super Computer Intelligence as an alternative name for artificial intelligence (AI), which also responds to U.S. President Donald J. Trump’s suggestion of renaming AI as Super Intelligence.

Etymologically speaking, “artificial” comes from the Latin “artificialis,” which breaks down to “ars” (that is, art, skill, or craft) and “facere” (that is, to make or do). In other words, it means “to do skill.” Intelligence comes from “intelligentia” (meaning understanding or discernment), derived from “intelligere,” meaning “to understand or comprehend.” Therefore, “artificial intelligence” merely translates to “understand skill making.”

Historically speaking, the term “AI” came to light through the Dartmouth Summer Research Project in 1956 organized by McCarthy, Minsky, and others.1 I argue that naming conventions are caught in social and historical contexts.2 In fact, McCarthy openly admitted that he preferred “AI” as a title for their summer project to avoid having to interact with or be overshadowed by Norbert Wiener, who cherished the term “cybernetics” instead. At the time, cybernetics (that is, control and communication in the animal and the machine)3 focused on mapping biologically inspired feedback mechanisms to analog hardware control loops, but McCarthy aimed for a naming convention that encapsulated logic, symbolic computation, and high-level programming. Historical reports4 indicate that McCarthy wanted a brand new captive name diverging from “automata theory” or “complex information processing” which could be more original and would attract financial backing. Later on, the name artificial intelligence would resonate well with Minsky’s theory of Society of Mind,5 which states that human intelligence can be considered as not a single, unified mechanism, but rather as an emergence born from the interactions of countless smaller, mindless parts called “agents,” which cannot think, feel, or understand but are manageable,5 hence can be engineered in a way that their outcome is attributed as artificial.

Philosophically speaking, the word “artificial” is the opposite of “natural.” For instance, an artificial flower contrasts a natural flower such that the former still shows beauty in its appearance, at least when seen from afar in perspective, but lacks the true nature of feeling, sensitivity, and appeal (beauty) found in a living flower when examined and touched closely. Thus one could argue that if we have called, or agreed upon, AI in its early beginnings, as computing, computer or machine intelligence, or intelligent machinery,6 then its ultimate expectations would never have existed because its technological wonders would have been known in simple practicalities as we may realize them now through image recognition, speech recognition, words sequence acquisition, etc. Simply saying, consider the facts that we have different kinds of intelligence (to name few: social intelligence, swarm intelligence, evolutionary intelligence, decentralized intelligence, biological intelligence, and neuro-symbolic AI), then we can notice with just a change of words that we can discreetly separate one kind of intelligence, those just mentioned, as one type of many others while not assuming that one is better than the other; they are all equal in terms of being intelligent in a way of at least solving a specific problem. In fact, all those forms of intelligence can be scaled and each one has its own limitations.

For example, Ant System7 inspired from ants’ decentralized colony intelligent behavior can solve the problem of finding a “good enough” optimal path from a food source to the nest. An ant colony fulfills such objective when scavenger ants find a food source and lay pheromones on such path; after that, all other ants will follow the same path and the whole colony is oriented towards the food source. This behavior has been translated to an algorithm and implemented in computer networks by directing data across Internet nodes that have minimal load or traffic.8 Therefore, ants can solve an optimization problem using decentralized intelligence; in such a framework there is no central server (such as a “big” ant directing the operations of the others), as each ant is following simple rules but the overall behavior of the whole colony is considered intelligent and their (the ants’) behavior is very efficient—intelligent—for such specific task.

In biological intelligence, the repository of knowledge and research is magnificent and endless. To name a few, we have synaptic plasticity, which helps us in building concepts and their associations by strengthening connections between neurons in the brain, as well as having dopamine levels that increase while we are anticipating an end goal. Those dopamine signals help us reinforce beneficial associations to achieve that goal.

Another example is evolutionary intelligence, where we have genetic algorithms mimicking the hereditary behavior of species’ chromosome crossovers and mutations in order to find the best fit (that is, the best solution) through many generations of mating. Such problems are challenging for humans to solve and their solution is promising using computer intelligence. Since all those forms of intelligence can be manifested and modeled using computers and acknowledging the fact that human intelligence would always be a peak endeavor, then why can’t we simply call their attempts as computer intelligence and therefore free us from the artificiality of the name artificial intelligence?

Finally, while writing this post, U.S. President Donald J. Trump, speaking before the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026, requested references to AI be changed to “Super Intelligence” (SI) in all U.S. documents.9 However, that notion is missing an identifier because any intelligence can be superb, even human intelligence. Besides, if SI means beyond human, then that is impossible because there will always be areas where humans can excel while intelligent machines will be lacking. For example, if we hide the data we gather on Mars or the Hadron Collider from the machines, then “they” will never be able to surpass us in comprehending Martian matter or the bosons, respectively.

In addition, considering the fact that current state-of-the-art AI algorithms require super computing power, then one could suggest a fair name: Super Computer Intelligence. This preserves the super-computing-power condition that is required for AI to function properly and possibly beyond our expectations, as well as its fundamental ground that is computer intelligence, which is the basic naming right for it.

References

1. McCarthy, J., Minsky, M. L., Rochester, N., and Shannon, C. E. A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, August 31, 1955. AI Magazine 27, 4 (2006), 12.

2. Derrida, J. and Spivak, G. C. Of Grammatology, Vol. 2, pp. 162-254. Johns Hopkins University Press, Baltimore (1976).

3. Wiener, N. and von Neumann, J. Cybernetics or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. Physics Today 2, 5 (1949), 33-34.

4. Radanliev, P. Artificial intelligence: reflecting on the past and looking towards the next paradigm shift. Journal of Experimental & Theoretical Artificial Intelligence 37, 7, 1045–1062.

5. Minsky, M., & Lee, J. The Society of Mind, Vol. 1. Simon and Schuster, New York (1988).

6. Turing, A. Intelligent Machinery (1948).

7. Dorigo, M., Colorni, A., and Maniezzo, V. Distributed optimization by ant colonies. In Proceedings of the first European conference on artificial life (1991), pp. 134-142.

8. Di Caro, G. and Dorigo, M. AntNet: Distributed stigmergetic control for communications networks. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 9 (1998), 317-365.

9. UN News. Trump defends military action against Iran, Venezuela, and calls for rebrand of AI. United Nations.


Mario Antoine Aoun is an ACM Senior Member who has been a Reviewer for ACM Computing Reviews since 2006. He has more than 25 years of computer programming experience and holds a Ph.D. in Cognitive Informatics from Canada’s Université du Québec à Montréal. His main research interest is memory modeling based on chaos theory and spiking neurons.

item.title: Click Fraud Beyond Bots: Why Better Models Are Not Enough
item.dc:creator: Harshit Agarwal
item.description: Click fraud has persisted not because detection engineering is inadequate, but because the economic incentives surrounding it reward fraud at every layer of the supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
In 2024, advertisers lost more than $100 billion to digital ad fraud, and Juniper Research projects the figure will reach $172 billion by 2028.7 Click fraud accounts for the largest share of that loss,7 and absolute costs have climbed relentlessly even as detection has improved. Not because the fraud rate is rising, but because global ad spending has expanded faster than defenses. No other engineering problem of this scale, with this level of sustained investment, has resisted solution for this long. That should give the computing community pause—not about whether detection technology is improving, but about whether detection technology is even the right lever.

The field’s dominant framing—treat invalid clicks as a classification problem, train a better model, deploy it—is not wrong; it is insufficient. Click fraud has persisted not because detection engineering is inadequate, but because the economic incentives surrounding it reward fraud at every layer of the supply chain. Detection operates on one layer. The incentives operate on all of them.

More Bots, Broken Audits

DoubleVerify detected 140% more CTV fraud schemes in Q1 2026 than a year earlier, identifying over 50 distinct bot variants in 2025 alone.5 The newest of these are agentic AI bots that mimic human browsing—scrolling, hesitating, navigating—specifically engineered to defeat the behavioral signals that current detection relies on.5 The measurement problem runs deeper than the fraud itself. A March 2025 Adalytics report described by The Wall Street Journal found that Integral Ad Science labeled known bot traffic as human 77% of the time across a 2019 to 2024 dataset; DoubleVerify missed the same bots 21% of the time.1 DoubleVerify disputed the methodology and filed a defamation suit; a securities class action followed in May 2025.4 But the core implication—that MRC accreditation does not guarantee bot blocking—was not substantively denied. Advertisers paying for third-party verification may be receiving less protection than they believe, and the companies measuring fraud carry the same structural incentive to under-report it that platform operators choose to tolerate.

Three Actors, Three Motives, and One Misconfigured Detector

The field treats click fraud as a single problem. It is not. Three distinct actors commit it for entirely different reasons, each requiring a different detection approach.

The first is the platform operator: generating fake traffic through bot networks or click farms costs a fraction of building legitimate traffic, yet earns the same per-click rate. This is rational behavior given the incentive structure, not a technical failure. A classifier trained on this type of fraud will systematically miss the other two.

The second actor is the competitor. In high-CPC (cost per click) categories such as legal, finance, and real estate, a single click can cost $50 to $100,3 and fraudulent clicks can account for up to 30% of total traffic in these verticals.3 Competitors direct bots or click farms at a rival’s ads to deplete their daily budget, removing them from the auction entirely. A 2025 PPC study found that 50% of marketers attributed nearly half of their fraudulent clicks to competitor activity.3 This variant is particularly hard to detect: it originates from real devices, often in the same geographic market as a legitimate audience. The distinguishing signal tends to be post-click behavior—sabotage clicks bounce immediately, real buyers navigate and linger.

The third actor is the fraudulent affiliate. Affiliate networks pay commission per click or conversion, creating a direct financial incentive for commission theft. Industry estimates place affiliate fraud at approximately 17% of affiliate traffic, costing around $3.4 billion annually.10 The Honey.com controversy of 2024 to 2025 brought one technique—cookie stuffing—to mainstream attention: the browser extension replaced legitimate affiliate cookies at checkout, claiming commissions on purchases it had no role in generating.9 More broadly, affiliate cloaking rose from 25% of fraud cases in 2022 to 45% by 2024.11 The detection signal is the commission-to-conversion ratio: a fraudulent affiliate accumulates clicks that evaporate before any purchase completes.

A classifier trained on platform-operator bot traffic will miss competitor sabotage—real devices, no purchase intent—and affiliate fraud—real clicks, stolen attribution. One detection system cannot be equally calibrated for all three.

An Arms Race, Not a Classification Problem

Standard detection trains on known bad traffic and catches what resembles it. Click fraud breaks this: the moment you improve your filter, fraudsters study what gets caught and adjust until they slip back through. Your false-negative rate is their calibration target—they need not defeat your system, only stay outside your detection zone. In practice, this probing tends to leave a trace: test traffic clusters just below your detection threshold, and a sudden spike there is often the first sign someone is mapping your defenses. Sometimes days pass before false-negative rates move. Watching the shape of your score distribution—not just the overall filter rate—turns their reconnaissance into your early warning.

The response is to use multiple independent signals that are hard to defeat simultaneously. Three signals worth combining in practice: click timing variance within a session (bots are either too mechanical or too erratic); scroll depth before clicking (bots head straight to the ad unit; real users wander first); and navigation path entropy (bots take direct routes; organic users meander). Evading one is straightforward; evading all three requires sustained human mimicry that is hard to automate at scale. More fundamentally, the goal is not to raise the detection bar—it is to make it invisible. Any threshold a fraudster can locate becomes one they can calibrate against. Overlapping signals with randomized decision elements make the boundary much harder to find.

Agentic AI bots challenge this directly. A scripted bot fails behavioral detection because its timing is mechanical, its paths direct, its scroll behavior absent. An agentic bot is goal-directed: given the objective ‘appear human to this classifier,’ it can observe which sessions get flagged, infer which signals triggered detection, and adapt until it passes. The signals above were calibrated against bots that did not know what was being measured. An agentic bot can learn what is being measured. Timing variance, scroll depth, and navigation entropy each lose their discriminating power the moment the adversary can optimize against them directly. The implication is a shift toward infrastructure signals—network fingerprints, device consistency across sessions, hardware attestation—that operate below the layer a bot’s learned behavior can influence. The arms race does not end; it moves to a layer that is harder to fake.

Why the Supply Chain Cannot Fix Itself

The economics of programmatic advertising reward fraud at every level. When a fraudulent platform operator inflates traffic with fake clicks, their reported numbers—click rates and impression volumes—look better than those of an honest operator who cleaned theirs up. Advertisers following the best-looking metrics send more budget to the fraudster and less to the honest operator, penalizing exactly the behavior that should be encouraged. The middlemen—ad exchanges and supply-side platforms that route transactions between advertisers and platform operators—earn a cut of every transaction regardless of traffic quality, so removing a high-volume fraudulent operator directly hurts their own revenue. Nobody in the chain has a financial reason to fix the problem, and the players with the most visibility into traffic quality have the least incentive to use it. The only pressure that can break this comes from advertisers. Requiring independent verification before spending, and negotiating refunds for confirmed invalid traffic, shifts the cost of fraud back onto the intermediaries who profit from tolerating it.

Platform operators in court. The pattern is consistent across two decades: the entity with the most visibility into traffic quality has the strongest financial reason not to look too closely. Google settled a click fraud suit for $90 million in 2006.8 Meta faced a class action over invisible ‘stealth clicks’ charged at full CPC rates.2 In 2026, the FTC sued Amazon, alleging its algorithm extracted an estimated $20 billion from advertisers through artificial auction manipulation.6

When Traffic Quality Fights Revenue

Inside every platform, fraud filtering creates an organizational conflict. Removing fake traffic makes reported clicks and sessions fall—which shows up on dashboards as a revenue problem, even when filtering is working exactly as intended. Without a prior agreement, this tends to play out the same way: the fraud team tightens a threshold; the revenue team points to falling numbers; the threshold gets loosened. The fix is a pre-agreed filtering rate that both teams commit to before the quarter begins, a number neither can change alone. When the rate holds, the threshold holds. When it is breached, both teams investigate together. In my experience, this structural alignment matters more than any model improvement: a better model inside a broken organizational structure gets overridden back to the same bad result.

Fixing click fraud requires working on two fronts the industry has treated as separate. On detection: watch how the mix of filtered traffic changes, not just the overall rate; test against fraud the system currently misses, not just what it already catches; and keep the detection boundary hidden so adversaries cannot calibrate against it. On incentives: advertiser pressure for mandatory refunds on confirmed invalid traffic, and regulatory enforcement of the kind the FTC is now pursuing against Amazon. Detection catches fraud after it occurs. Changing incentives removes the motivation to commit it in the first place. Until the incentive front receives the same investment as the detection front, click fraud engineering will remain what it has been for two decades: always improving, never arriving.

Disclosure:  I used generative AI tools for limited editorial assistance, including language refinement and structural review. I independently reviewed and verified the content and references and take full responsibility for the final version.

2. ClassAction.org. Facebook Inflates CPC Ad Prices by ‘Stealth’ Clicking on the Ads Itself, Class Action Says. (2024).

3. ClickPatrol. PPC Click Fraud Study 2025: Key Statistics, Industry Insights, and Prevention Strategies (2025).

4. DoubleVerify Sues Adalytics, Jury Trial Demanded, MediaPost (May 16, 2025); DoubleVerify Class Action Lawsuit: Shareholder Portfolio Decimation After the Truth Emerges. ClassActionLawyerTN (2025).

5. DoubleVerify. Must-CTV: Streaming’s Shift From Promise to Performance (2026 Global Insights Report). Summarized in CTV fraud schemes up 140% as AI arms both sides of the fight. PPC Land (2026).

6. FTC sues Amazon, accusing the e-commerce giant of misleading advertisers. CNBC (August 31, 2026).

7. Juniper Research. Quantifying the Cost of Ad Fraud: 2023–2028. Research whitepaper (2024).

8. Google Agrees To $90 Million Settlement In Class Action Lawsuit Over Click Fraud. Search Engine Watch (March 8, 2006).

9. PPC Land. Honey drops to 14 million Chrome users amid ongoing affiliate scandal (2025).

10. TrafficGuard. The State of Affiliate Fraud in 2025 (2025).

11. Affiliate cloaking is behind 45% of fraud—here’s how to beat it. Search Engine Land (2025).
